newsitem.title: USA: Clinton reshaped his presidency to win second term.
newsitem.headline: Clinton reshaped his presidency to win second term.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, who likes to call himself "The Comeback Kid," rebounded from a chaotic first two years in office marked by personal and political disasters to reshape his presidency and win re-election on Tuesday.

The 50-year-old Democrat who has spent 22 years running for political offices scored a major victory in what he called his last election -- becoming the first Democrat to be re-elected to the presidency since Franklin Roosevelt in 1944.

Grayer after four years of swiftly changing fortunes, the Democratic "baby-boomer" displayed optimism and limitless energy on the campaign trail even as his opponents, Republican Bob Dole and Reform Party candidate Ross Perot, hammered away at his ethics, his character and his associates.

Voters put aside their doubts about Clinton, giving him a vote of confidence because of his economic record and compassionate image. Early analysis of the results showed Clinton won largely because of the support of women voters.

Sobered by the Republican takeover of Congress in 1994, Clinton set the tone for his re-election drive at the start of the year in his annual State of the Union speech when he portrayed himself as the leader of the mainstream political centre and proclaimed: "The era of big government is over."

As the year progressed he co-opted many Republican issues -- welfare reform and crime-fighting for example -- to run as a centrist Democrat. But perhaps most noteworthy was the way he turned to his own advantage the pledge of 73-year-old Dole to be "a bridge to the past" of traditional values.

Calling himself the candidate for the 21st century, Clinton would say at his rallies: "Are we going to build a bridge to the future or a bridge to the past?" It managed to remind voters indirectly of Dole's advanced age.

As recently as late 1994, Clinton seemed destined to be a mediocre one-term president as Republicans rode a wave of voter discontent to take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives for the first time in 40 years. Clinton was reduced to defending himself publicly against accusations that he had become "irrelevant."

But then Republicans handed him a free ride back from the political wilderness, pushing national spending cuts many people viewed as too harsh for the poor and elderly and too rough on education and environmental protections.

If Clinton had trouble making people believe he had core convictions, the Republicans gave him something to be against. Since he had never really stopped campaigning after his 1992 victory, he was off and running against "the extremists" in control of Congress.

Clinton was mired in controversy as soon as the elation of his January 1993 inauguration faded and he heads into his second terms with many of those controversies still swirling around him and being investigated.

There was the firing of White House travel office workers, his opening the military to homosexuals, several botched appointments to key positions and accusations about the Clintons' Whitewater investment from the 1980s in Arkansas. The darkest hour came in July 1993 when his boyhood friend, deputy White House counsel Vince Foster, committed suicide.

The after-shocks still ripple through the White House. And independent counsel Kenneth Starr's Whitewater investigation is still going strong, guaranteeing pressures from that quarter will continue in a second Clinton term.

A plan for a radical revamping of the U.S. health care system, led by Clinton's wife, Hillary, fed into suspicions Clinton was at heart a big-government liberal and became the biggest political disaster of his first term.

Many Americans surveyed in polls said they had questions about Clinton's character and 52 percent in election day exit polls said they did not trust him, but the question marks were not enough to keep him from easily beating Dole.

Talkative and supremely self-confident, Clinton stirs strong emotions both positive and negative. This was exemplified during a recent jog on a California beach when he was denounced by one woman as a "yellow-bellied, draft-dodging liar" while another woman shouted, "We love you."

Clinton was also blessed by a prosperous U.S. economy. Many analysts said this was the cyclical product of various forces but he attributed it to his own economic policies -- never mentioning they included a huge tax increase. "We are better off than we were four years ago," he said.
Born on Aug. 19, 1946, in tiny Hope, Arkansas, Clinton got a taste of -- and for -- the presidency with a group of teenagers who met President John Kennedy at the White House.

In high school, he tooled around in a big Buick and pretended he was Elvis Presley. He later avoided the Vietnam War draft by using student advantages, attended Georgetown University, was a Rhodes Scholar at Oxford in the late 1960s and took a law degree at Yale. He met his wife, Hillary, there. Their daughter, Chelsea, is 16.
